profile.name: Tītī tōrea
profile.tagline: A traditional Māori stick game and rhythmic dance of hand-eye coordination
profile.insight: Played to a beat of three, tītī tōrea challenges players to throw wooden sticks between partners, a practice used by Māori warriors to build hand-eye coordination.
profile.profile: Tītī tōrea is a traditional Māori game and Polynesian dance performed with wooden sticks called tītī. Typically played by two or more participants, the game involves throwing sticks back and forth to a structured rhythm, commonly set in a beat of three. Historically, it served as training for male warriors to sharpen their hand-eye coordination. Today, it is performed across Polynesia and featured at cultural venues such as the Polynesian Cultural Center in Honolulu, O'ahu, Hawai'i.
profile.profile_long:
Tītī tōrea originates as a Māori game and Polynesian dance tradition centered on physical dexterity and rhythmic coordination. Participants utilize wooden sticks known as tītī, exchanging them between partners or within group formations. The tradition carries deep historical roots in training male warriors, who relied on the rapid exchange of sticks to refine hand-eye coordination, reaction times, and focus required for martial agility.

The performance of tītī tōrea is defined by its rhythmic foundation, typically executed to a beat of three. Players sit or stand facing one another, tapping and throwing the sticks in synchronized patterns aligned with musical accompaniment. Among the traditional and popular songs performed alongside tītī tōrea are 'E Papa Waiari' and 'Hurihuri', which establish the meter and cadence for the players' movements.

While rooted in traditional Māori practice, tītī tōrea is widely performed across Polynesia. Beyond traditional community contexts, it is routinely demonstrated to international audiences, such as at the Polynesian Cultural Center located in Honolulu on the island of O'ahu, Hawai'i. Through these performances, the game functions as both a living cultural craft and an educational presentation of Polynesian musicality and partner dynamics.

Technique in tītī tōrea focuses heavily on stick handling and paired rhythm work. Players coordinate exact release and catch points while maintaining the three-beat musical structure. Although exact physical postures and variations beyond the stick-throwing mechanic are not fully detailed in available documentation, the tradition relies on continuous interaction, rhythmic precision, and spatial awareness between partners.

sections.origins_and_history: Tītī tōrea is a Māori game and Polynesian dance tradition. Traditionally, some forms of tītī tōrea were utilized to practice hand-eye coordination and improve the physical preparedness of male warriors.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The practice is executed by two or more players who throw wooden sticks, known as tītī, to each other. The game typically follows a beat of three, requiring participants to maintain continuous hand-eye coordination and rhythmic synchronization as sticks are passed across the pair or group.
sections.music_and_instruments: Tītī tōrea performances are set to rhythmic musical accompaniment, usually following a beat of three. Popular songs performed alongside the stick game include 'E Papa Waiari' and 'Hurihuri'. The primary sound-producing objects during the dance are the wooden sticks (tītī) themselves as they are struck and caught.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performances take place in community spaces across Polynesia, as well as institutional cultural settings such as the Polynesian Cultural Center in Honolulu, O'ahu, Hawai'i, United States. Specific traditional dress details are not described in sources.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Historically associated with warrior training and skill development, tītī tōrea serves as a display of dexterity, teamwork, and musical timing. In contemporary settings, it functions as a popular performance and recreational game across Polynesia.
sections.regional_variants: Tītī tōrea is performed in Aotearoa New Zealand as well as across broader Polynesia, including stage and educational demonstrations in Honolulu, Hawai'i.
sections.lineage: Classified as both a traditional Māori game and a Polynesian dance type involving rhythmic stick handling.

basic_steps: Hold wooden sticks (tītī) securely in hand.
Establish a rhythmic pattern usually based on a beat of three.
Throw sticks across to a partner on designated counts while receiving incoming sticks.
teaching.rhythm: Usually set to a beat of three.
teaching.formation: Two or more players facing each other.
teaching.level_notes: Beginners focus on simple partner stick throws on the three-beat meter before accelerating tempo.

music_profile.musical_form: Strophic vocal accompaniment with stick percussion
music_profile.sound_description: A rhythmic blend of vocal melody accompanied by the sharp percussive clicking and catching sound of wooden sticks thrown in a three-beat count.

movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Hand-eye coordinated catching and throwing of wooden sticks (tītī).
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Two or more players positioned together to throw wooden sticks back and forth.
movement_profile.partnering: Paired or multi-player stick throwing and catching.

social_formats.description: Played by two or more players throwing wooden sticks to each other.

episode_brief.title_hook: Sticks, Beats, and Warriors: The Rhythm of Tītī Tōrea
episode_brief.logline: Discover how a traditional Māori stick game transforms hand-eye warrior training into a mesmerizing Polynesian dance of precision and beat.
beats: Introduction to the wooden sticks (tītī) and the historical role in training male warriors.
Demonstration of the core beat of three and initial stick-handling mechanic.
Pair formation showing stick exchange between two players.
Musical pairing with traditional songs 'E Papa Waiari' and 'Hurihuri'.
Performance setting at the Polynesian Cultural Center in Honolulu.

lesson_ladder.goal: Master stick holding and solo tapping to a beat of three.
drills: Tap sticks on floor on counts 1 and 2, click together on count 3.

lesson_ladder.goal: Execute single stick exchanges with a partner.
drills: Pass right stick straight across to partner on count 3.

lesson_ladder.goal: Full two-stick simultaneous exchange set to 'E Papa Waiari'.
drills: Simultaneous cross-throw on count 3 maintaining steady vocal tempo.

visual_motifs: Wooden sticks striking and crossing in mid-air
Paired players making synchronized eye contact
Rhythmic hands catching wooden tītī on the third beat
episode_brief.instructor_persona: An engaging, focused Polynesian cultural educator emphasizing precision, rhythm, and partner connection.
episode_brief.music_cue: Traditional vocal track of 'E Papa Waiari' with steady rhythmic emphasis on a beat of three.
